lines.text: Every year, lakhs of students join AICTE-approved institutions.
Which of them were actually admitted, and how many seats did they fill?
Today, most institutions report totals.
A total can't show who is enrolled, whether one student is counted twice, or whether a programme went over its approved intake.
This register keeps a record for every student, keyed to their APAAR ID.
It opens like a familiar government portal, with text-size controls and a skip link.
Every role has its own account, and all the data you'll see is synthetic.
An institution sees its seat position, programme by programme.
Green cells are occupied seats. The dark line is the approved intake.
Supernumerary categories are counted separately, each against its own cap.
Submitting starts with the institution's usual spreadsheet.
Sixteen rows are checked against twenty-five named rules before anything is saved.
Five are valid, two need review, and nine have errors.
Every error says how to fix it.
This APAAR ID isn't in the registry. But one near-variant matches the student's name and date of birth, so the system suggests it.
Nothing changes until the user accepts it.
Other rows are fixed in place, and a duplicate row is simply left out.
Zero errors. Fifteen rows ready to commit.
Before committing, the user sees exactly what will happen to each programme's seats.
The moment they commit, AICTE's national register updates. No reload.
Excess admission is easier to prevent than to find later.
Before admitting one more student, Godavari runs a seat check.
The answer is clear: this would exceed the approved intake by one.
If the institution uploads anyway, the projection shows four seats over, in red.
The records are still accepted. Blocking them would only reward under-reporting.
Instead, flags open for AICTE: excess intake, a category over its cap, and a student already active elsewhere.
That last flag involves two institutions, and each sees only its own side.
Godavari sees another AICTE-approved institution, identity withheld. AICTE sees both.
A flag means a person should look. It never says fraud.
AICTE asks for clarification, and every step is recorded with a note.
When Godavari cancels four duplicate admissions, the excess flag closes itself, and the system logs exactly why.
Review priority tells AICTE where to look first, with a reason for every point.
And identity matching, tuned for Indian names, finds the same person under different spellings, then explains why.
Institutions can issue a signed digital record.
The student decides what to share: institution, programme and status, but not their APAAR ID.
Anyone can verify it, without an account. All six checks pass.
Change a single value, and the check fails.
And if the institution revokes it, the verifier sees when, and why.
An employer can also ask through the register, but only with the student's consent.
The student sees exactly which fields will be shared, and allows it.
The employer gets those fields, and nothing more.
Every action is written to a tamper-evident audit chain, and an auditor can verify it in one click.
One register. Every seat accounted for. Every record verifiable.
Built for AICTE, problem statement S I H two six two six three.
